title: Can Agentic Robotics Solve Robotics’ Data-Scaling Problem?
summary:
Robotics companies are investing heavily in the belief that data will solve the most difficult problems in robotics. Once AI systems have ingested enough data from human demonstrations, the thinking goes, robots will be able to perform the vast majority of the manual tasks that humans now do. There are even robotics companies that exist solely to collect training data and sell it to other robotics companies in pursuit of this goal.

But whether data will finally bring us general-purpose robots is an open question. Nobody knows how much data would be necessary, what kind of data is important, or whether something else might be missing. And there are other problems with a reliance on massive amounts of data: The resulting AI algorithms are essentially black boxes, which despite their high performance are difficult or impossible for humans to understand. This characteristic is becoming increasingly concerning in commercial deployments, where robots must be flexible, reliable, and safe.

At the 2026 Conference on Robot Learning this week, University of California, Berkeley and Nvidia are jointly announcing a new approach to using AI to program robots for everyday practical tasks in industrial environments. Called agentic robotics, this technique leverages the latest advances in AI coding tools while in some sense bringing robotics back to its roots—achieving a fundamental understanding of how a robot works, and then writing human-readable code to get it to do useful things, no data (and no humans) required.

The Data Problem

For decades, robots were programmed with model-based methods, meaning that their behavior was based on a detailed understanding (or model) of the physics and mathematics underlying the robot and its environment. Roboticists would first develop these models, and then write painstakingly detailed code telling their robots how to act. The resulting hand-tuned robotic systems could operate fast and reliably, but this approach has fallen out of favor because it requires both human time and human expertise. It’s much easier to just feed a huge amount of human demonstration data into a machine learning system, and the results that come out are both adaptable and reliable—up to a point.

“The imitation-learning paradigm has hit a plateau,” explains Ken Goldberg, a professor of robotics at UC Berkeley whose lab is presenting a paper on agentic robotics at this week’s conference. “It’s promising for things like home robots, where speed and reliability are less of an issue. But for industrial applications, it’s very hard to get the reliability that industry requires.” Goldberg, who is also a cofounder of the industrial robotics company Ambi Robotics, has experienced this problem firsthand, as have other companies that he’s been working with, including Siemens and Bosch. “You get good performance from data initially, but then things go wrong. So you start giving it more data. But then other things go wrong. It’s not clear that adding more data is going to get you there.”

The hope, according to Goldberg, is that with enough data, robots will somehow just start to work reliably, since that was the case with ChatGPT. “That’s what people have been counting on, and why investors are pouring money into these companies,” says Goldberg. “But everybody’s getting a little nervous that we haven’t hit that convergence point.”

How Agentic Robotics Works

The reason why language models like ChatGPT are so successful is that they can train on data at the scale of the internet. There is no dataset for robotics that approaches that scale, and while robotics companies are desperately attempting to generate the data that they think they need, it’s a slow, expensive process. Agentic robotics, a term popularized by Goldberg along with Spencer Huang, director of product for robotics at Nvidia, is an attempt to turn programming robots from a data problem into a coding problem, which can directly leverage the scale of language models.

“This is really something that’s accelerated in the past year,” Goldberg says. “The quality of agentic coding has become so good that using them to write code for robots is now viable.”

Because agentic robotics is based on large language models, it’s easy to use—you can use natural language to tell the robot what to do. One example used by the UC Berkeley researchers was asking a robotic arm to pack groceries into a bag. First, this relatively complex (for a robot) task is decomposed into simpler subtasks, each of them assigned to a separate coding agent. In LLM-based software, a coding agent is an autonomous AI system that can plan, write, test, and modify software with minimal human intervention. You might have one individual agent tasked with perception to identify the groceries and the bag, a second focused on object manipulation with the arm’s gripper, and a third working on transporting objects with the arm once they’ve been grasped.

“We have all these robotics tools we’ve been building for the last couple decades,” explains Huang. “The problem was that a human had to go and write the code themselves. But object classifiers, pose estimation, task and motion planning, trajectory generation—everything is already there.” The coding agents can directly leverage all of that existing data contained within their language models to generate code of their own, tailored to their specific tasks.

Solving the Simulation Bottleneck

Once the agents have a plausible framework, they run their code in a simulation and see what happens, much like a human would. They can change starting conditions, identify failures, refine the code, and keep iterating until they’ve got a successful program. Of course, code that works in simulation can only ever be as versatile and reliable as the simulation is.

“Simulations are nontrivial to build,” Goldberg explains. The more accurate the simulation has the potential to be, the more parameters there are that need to be configured to achieve and maintain that accuracy, typically by a human on a task-by-task basis. Goldberg decided to try giving an AI agent direct access to these simulation parameters, and instructing it to match the simulation to a video of the real world.

“It gave us goose bumps. It was matching the whole environment, the lighting, the background, all these things that are super tedious to do. We would never have done that, but the agent did. Side by side, it was very hard to tell the difference between the simulation and the video.”

Nevertheless, no matter how good a simulated environment looks, navigating the gap between that environment and the real world is still an unsolved challenge for the robotics community, says Torsten Kroeger, chief science officer at Alphabet’s company Intrinsic. Kroeger, who is not directly involved in this research, continued: “I’m saying this respectfully, but there’s just no physics engine out there that can accurately model physical contact with the world.” But as with a team of human coders, the agents can troubleshoot when things inevitably don’t work quite right. The agents’ ability to work on the simulation itself offers significant advantages, because the agents can be fed video of a failed task with the goal of updating the simulation to match, while the coding agents then iterate to fix the problem.

As with anything done by AI, Huang is well aware that agents writing code for robots will have their flaws. “We all know that AI agents can create slop,” Huang says. “In order to counter that, we use adversarial agent setups—where one agent designs something and another agent tries to rip it apart and find flaws.”

In UC Berkeley’s testing, agentic robotics approaches were able to reach success rates of up to 99 percent, matching human hand-engineered performance, even in tasks where baseline imitation-learning techniques saw success rates of only 20 percent. But as Goldberg points out, agentic robotics is not just about performance but also efficiency and safety. “You’re using an off-the-shelf coding agent. You don’t need to collect any data. And the agent is generating code that you can actually understand and fix if necessary.”

Real-World Agentic Robotics

In the immediate future, the sweet spot for practical agentic robotics will be industrial manufacturing and manipulation tasks that require robust precision and accuracy, says Huang. “Right now, some of our partners in the semiconductor space need to place components within 0.3 millimeters. There’s no way you’re going to get something like GR00T [Nvidia’s humanoid-development platform] to do that today with any semblance of repeatability and robustness. What you get with agentic robotics is near-term applications.”

But the real value, Huang says, is in adapting to change. “At Wistron in Taiwan [which manufactures baseboards for Nvidia GPUs], every time they add a new product, it takes a minimum of 8 hours to retask one robot. With agentic robotics, retasking takes a minute or two instead.”

Moving agentic robotics beyond these fairly well-constrained use cases may be difficult, but Huang sees this technique as a gateway toward more complex tasks. “Agentic robotics can generate tons of good-quality robotic code, which is data that we can use for training the next model.” Such code generation is only an iterative step toward a general-purpose capability, but Huang believes that agentic robotics may help redefine the very meaning of general intelligence in the context of robotics. “My thesis is that general intelligence for robotics will first come in the form of an agent orchestrating a mix of conventional technologies and specialized policies. To a human, it looks like general intelligence because the agent is coordinating everything under the hood.”

Intrinsic’s Kroeger is more cautious about placing trust in agents. “In the context of safety and security, how do we know that these agents are really doing the right thing all the time? It’s the alignment problem. A human engineer can review everything, but the challenge will be once we start putting our trust in these agents. I can imagine that this will become a relevant conversation for the industry.”

For now, Goldberg is focused on working with real companies to put agentic robotics into practice. A series of benchmarks for agentic robotics developed with Nvidia Isaac Lab-Arena and the Newton physics engine will help researchers evaluate agent performance. “I don’t want to say that we have the solution, but I’m very excited about it,” he says. Adds Huang: “It’s a pivotal change in the way we’re doing things.”

title: Are Drone Ports the Next Annoying Tech Neighbor?
summary:
Rick and Marcia LeCompte loved to watch the Cooper’s hawks that frequented a sweet-gum tree in their yard in Baton Rouge, La. But this October, the hawks were gone. Marcia LeCompte is convinced the birds were scared away by the same flying robots that have been vexing the couple since early September. The noise had them spending less time outside in their garden, and even inside their home, they couldn’t escape the near-constant buzzing. Angry and feeling harassed, the LeComptes began to think about moving.

The problem: delivery drones.


Amazon’s MK30 delivery drones are large and must fly near the ground when making deliveries.Annabel Lee-Ellis/Press Association/AP Images

Last August, Amazon Prime Air began flying its MK30 drones from a distribution center 3.2 kilometers (2 miles) from the LeComptes’ home. People in the neighborhood first noticed just a few of the drones, flying high (U.S. regulations authorize drones to fly at up to 120 meters (400 feet)). But a couple of weeks later, they felt as if drones were everywhere, and often flying much lower.

The high-pitched whine of rotors was what bothered them the most, says Blake Fugler, who lives in the same neighborhood. It sounded as if a neighbor was constantly using a weed whacker for hours every day, he says. Acoustic research has found that the noise of drone rotors is more annoying than that of cars, airplanes, and other familiar background sounds. Once flights became frequent, the noise made people miserable. “Outside the house on a Saturday between 9 and 10 a.m., I counted a drone every 48 seconds,” says Fugler’s partner, Cristina Boone.

Delivery Drone Concerns

Neighbors had concerns about drones buzzing over playgrounds, schools, and services at the local cemetery; a drone that made a forced landing on the median of a busy highway; and the fact that drones are equipped with cameras. Then word spread about Amazon’s plans as reported in the FAA’s Environmental Assessment for the facility: “Operations would occur between 6 a.m. and 10:30 p.m., with 100 of the 1,000 daily delivery operations (10%) occurring during the period from 6 a.m. to 7 a.m. and 10 p.m. to 10:30 p.m.”

As they quickly expand their operations around the world, delivery-drone companies—including Alphabet’s Wing Aviation, Amazon Prime Air, Doordash Air, JD Logistics, Manna Aero, Matternet, Meituan, Zipline, and more, say their flying robots are quiet, safe, and unobtrusive. Massive expansion is planned for the near future. In Asia, for example, Meituan launched its latest “low-altitude delivery network’’ in September in Shanghai, while JD continues to expand drone service in rural China. In the U.S., Zipline and Uber have announced a partnership with the goal of 1 million drone deliveries a day by the end of 2029. Wing aims to have 270 U.S. drone hubs operating by the end of 2027. And Amazon Prime Air, which currently delivers in about 85 municipalities in the U.S., says it plans to serve 500 by the end of 2026.

A Wing “nest” of delivery drones in a parking lot.Wing

Yet as the companies aggressively scale up, “the public outreach piece has probably been more of an afterthought than it should have been,” says David Ison, a specialist in Emerging Aviation Technologies and Land Use Compatibility at the Washington State Department of Transportation, who has worked on the state’s drone-hub land-use guidelines. “I think what companies assumed is everybody would be cheering that they could get things delivered by drone in half an hour.”

Companies tout drone delivery as a way to do good. Zipline has delivered blood plasma and vaccines in Africa. Material that Wing provided at public meetings in the Dallas Fort Worth area says its deliveries there have saved more than 1,000 tonnes of carbon that would have been emitted by delivery trucks. For businesses, drone delivery is supposed to offer faster service and reduce costs, although whether drones are actually less costly is a complex question that depends on a variety of interconnected factors.

The commercial and philanthropic use cases make for an unusual sales pitch, notes Ison. “It’s a lot easier argument to make when you’re saying you’re delivering blood to an accident site than when you’re delivering a fidget toy.” But instead of being impressed, people troubled by drones say they feel they’re being pushed around by a distant corporation. “It’s the same way data centers strong-arm communities,” says Boone.

Newly arrived drone launch sites have triggered similar fears from China to France to Australia to within many communities in the United States, including suburban Detroit; Richardson, Texas; Glendale, Ariz.; East Cobb, Ga.; Maplewood, Mo.; and Westborough, Mass. The response has sometimes been enough to shut down local drone operations completely.

An early Wing trial in 2018 in suburban Canberra, Australia, shut down a few months later, after activists formed an opposition group and rallied support in Parliament. In response, the company “fundamentally reshaped [its] engineering priorities, flight operations, and community-engagement strategy,” says Jessie Poole-Strang, Wing’s communications lead. It redesigned its drones to reduce noise, changed flight-path algorithms, and now makes efforts to familiarize people with its robots before a facility opens.

Communities Take Action

Still, legal and political campaigns against drones continue to arise. On 28 September, 15 U.S. states and Harris County, Texas, sued the FAA to stop it from easing its environmental assessment rules for drone sites, which are key to local government control. In April, the Cobb County Board of Commissioners in Georgia denied a zoning request for a Wing drone facility there.

In response to the Cobb County complaints, a Wing spokesperson said the company was hearing “positive feedback” from people in Cobb County. Similarly, Amazon representatives have said most feedback from customers about drone delivery is “overwhelmingly positive,” and Zipline has encouraged at least one local official to refer to drone delivery as a “totally normal part of life.”

Wing’s drone is smaller and lighter than some other delivery drones.Wing

But fundamental concerns remain. “There are safety, noise, and visual-pollution issues with all these platforms,” Ison says, noting that it’s important not to lump all drone technologies together. For example, concerns about accidents are more relevant to Amazon’s MK-30 drone, which weighs almost 36 kilograms (80 pounds), than to Wing’s largest drone, which weighs less than 11 kilograms (25 pounds) with its payload included. Another safety consideration: Wing and Zipline, he notes, lower their packages to the ground via a tether, which leaves the craft higher in the air than Amazon’s, which must get low enough to drop its load without damage.

And Ison expects continuing disputes about noise. This is because U.S. law is not settled on people’s rights to airspace just above their property. “Maybe someone says, ‘You can’t fly over my house’ or ‘I want you to pay me to fly over my house,’ ” Ison says. “That is a murky area that is going to have to be worked out in court.”

For now, in the Baton Rouge neighborhood where the LeComptes, Fugler, and Boone live, the skies have calmed. Their councilman says Amazon Prime Air has responded to the outcry by rerouting 70 percent of drone flights elsewhere, although since the drones are not allowed to fly over highways, that likely means other residential neighborhoods. As of late October, LeCompte says she is now seeing, “two or three a day” over their home, although on a trip to the bank a few miles away, she counted eight in 20 minutes. “Sorry for those folks, but I thank Amazon for clearing our sky.”

title: Your Robot’s Safety Functions Already Work. What If the Input Lies?
summary:
This article is brought to you by VicOne.

A mobile robot slows for someone in a hallway. A collaborative arm eases its movement as a worker approaches. A humanoid pauses to let a person pass. Each response depends on information about the robot or its surroundings: a distance reading, a position estimate, or a stop signal.

But what happens when one of those inputs is wrong, and the robot still responds exactly as designed? The mobile robot reads the hallway as clear while someone is still there. The arm estimates that the worker is farther away. The humanoid does not receive a stop signal as a person crosses its path.

In each case, a fault could cause that mismatch. So could deliberate manipulation.

At VicOne LAB R7, we examine how manipulated inputs can change robot behavior — and what that means for the systems meant to keep people safe.

How an untrusted input can change a robot’s behavior

A robot does more than measure its surroundings. It may interpret what it sees and hears to decide what to do next. Information placed in its environment can therefore influence its actions.

Published research shows how this can happen. In a study of vision-language-action (VLA) models, a patch in a camera’s view reduced task success in simulated robot tests. FreezeVLA found that an adversarial image could cause tested models to ignore later instructions. Although the studies used different methods, both demonstrate how visual input can interfere with a robot’s intended task.

In a robot-dog test using Gemma 4 E4B, text on a poster was treated as an instruction and changed the robot’s movement.

VicOne LAB R7 also tested how untrusted inputs could change robot behavior. In a robot-dog test using Gemma 4 E4B, text on a poster was treated as an instruction and changed the robot’s movement. In a separate hospital-service-robot simulation using Nemotron on NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin, crafted audio that is inaudible to people changed the robot’s simulated behavior. The assigned tasks did not change; the inputs did.

In a VicOne LAB R7 test, text on a poster changed a robot dog’s movement, illustrating how a crafted input can turn an unlikely outcome into a repeatable attack.VicOne

Safety-related decisions have inputs too

An independent protective system may still stop a dangerous action. But that system also depends on information: readings, estimates, and messages that tell it when to intervene. What happens if one of those inputs is manipulated?

At a robotics bug bounty event, VicOne LAB R7 researchers injected a ROS 2/DDS message into a robot that organizers expected to remain still under a safe-control setting. The robot moved.

A humanoid’s balance controller offers another example. If it relies on a vulnerable gyroscope, sound at the sensor’s resonant frequency could distort its reported rotation. The controller might correct for a tilt that never occurred. Researchers demonstrated the underlying acoustic attack against drones with vulnerable gyroscopes. The research did not demonstrate the same attack chain causing a humanoid to fall.

Other protections could interrupt either chain. The question for safety and security teams is whether those protections detect the danger independently or depend on the same manipulated information.

Figure 1. VicOne maps how accidental faults and deliberate cyber manipulation can lead to similar robot safety outcomes, from loss of control to physical harm.VicOne

Deliberate attacks challenge safety assumptions

A safety assessment may treat a combination of accidental faults as unlikely. Deliberate manipulation changes that assumption. An attacker can choose when to introduce a false input and repeat the same trigger. That does not make harm inevitable, but it may change how cyber risks should be assessed.

Redundant sensors also need an adversarial test. If one action can affect both inputs, their agreement may offer less reassurance than expected. In autonomous driving research, a crafted physical object misled a system combining camera and LiDAR perception. The study does not establish a weakness in a particular robot, but it shows why teams should test whether one manipulation can affect several checks at once.

Cyber threats add intent to the safety equation, so risk assessments based on accidental faults must be revisited to account for attacks that can be timed and repeated.

Security testing strengthens robot safety evidence

Safety teams set limits for speed, protective distances, and permitted operating areas. The evidence behind those limits should also show what happens when the information used to enforce them is deliberately manipulated.

That evidence can also support assessments against applicable requirements. China’s GB/T 45502-2025 addresses information security for service robots. IEC TS 63074 examines security threats that could affect safety-related control systems. The EU Machinery Regulation, which applies from January 20, 2027, includes requirements to protect safety-relevant systems and data against corruption. Each has its own scope, and teams still need evidence for their robot’s design and operating conditions.

Figure 2. Cybersecurity strengthens robot safety evidence throughout the lifecycle. VicOne helps teams test safety limits against manipulation before deployment and monitor the conditions behind safe behavior in operation.VicOne

Before deployment, safety and security engineers can compare normal and adversarial scenarios against the same safety limits. During operation, they can monitor for changes to software, models, sensor signals, or behavior that may call earlier results into question. Any response to suspicious behaviors should follow policies approved by the safety team.

VicOne supports that work across the robot lifecycle. Through the Robotic Hacking Community, VicOne LAB R7 works with researchers to investigate how cyber threats can change robot behavior. VicOne’s Radeis helps teams validate potential effects before deployment, while Rthena provides visibility into risks and behavior during operation.

Five questions safety and security teams should answer together

The central test is whether a robot’s safeguards still protect people when the information they rely on is manipulated. Safety and security teams can begin by tracing the inputs behind each protective decision, challenging them, and revisiting the evidence as the robot changes. They can start with these five questions:

1. What does each protective function read? Map the readings, estimates, messages, and confirmations. Identify which safeguards operate independently of the robot’s AI decisions.

2. How does that information arrive? Check how inputs are produced, transmitted, authenticated where appropriate, and handled when they are missing or implausible.

3. What happens if an input is manipulated? Test false distances, drifting position estimates, and other relevant scenarios against the robot’s safety limits.

4. Can one action mislead several inputs? Check whether sensor fusion or seemingly independent safeguards share a point of failure.

5. When should the evidence be revisited? Reassess after changes to software, models, sensors, or operating conditions. Agree on bounded responses to suspicious behavior with the safety team in advance.

The goal is not only to show that a protective function works. Teams also need evidence that it remains protective when the information behind its decision is wrong or deliberately manipulated — and that another safeguard can catch the resulting hazard when needed. As robots change, that evidence needs to change with them.

For a deeper look how cybersecurity can affect robot safety, download our white paper “Why Robot Safety Depends on Cybersecurity: Protecting the Information That Safety Decisions Rely On.”

title: The Robot I Didn’t Expect to Build
summary:
Agility Robotics, the company I cofounded out of my robotics lab at Oregon State University in 2015, has just launched Digit 5. It’s designed to be the first humanoid robot that can safely and economically do useful work at scale, allowing us to bring tens of thousands of humanoid workers into the real world. Engineered to lift 23-kilogram bins onto high shelves and with a battery that can run for 90 minutes on a 9-minute charge, Digit 5’s goal is to handle heavy warehouse tasks shift after shift, filling the need for labor in jobs that are too physically stressful or too dull for humans to want to do.

Digit 5 is what Agility has been working toward for over a decade. But the robot is heavy and bulky, lacking the graceful natural motion of its predecessors, and it’s farther than I thought possible from the robot I dreamed of building when I started this company. To deliver a useful commercial product, Agility has taken a path that is very different from what I first imagined.

From ATRIAS to Digit

My dream has always been to build robots that combine locomotion and manipulation to move through the world and interact with it as people do. I seek a mastery of motion, achieved through devices designed to navigate the constraints of physics with elegance. When I started the Dynamic Robotics Laboratory at Oregon State in 2008, we began with a theory derived from decades of work in biomechanics: that a simple “spring-mass” model (a body supported by legs that act like springs) should be able to reproduce every known walking and running gait found in animals.

We put theory into practice by building the bipedal robot ATRIAS—short for “Assume The Robot Is A Sphere,” a joke among physicists about reducing a complex system to its simplest possible form. ATRIAS looked like a large microwave on stilts because it was only intended to demonstrate the physics of human walking and running. This was the first glimmer of achieving my dream; even though ATRIAS wasn’t designed to look like us, it still seemed natural, and even somehow alive, when it settled into a walking gait.

With the success of ATRIAS, the barriers to progress shifted from scientific to engineering and organizational, and a startup company seemed like the way to bridge the gap from a one-off research concept to an actual robotic product. I felt confident of two things: that I would be able to build robots that could go where people go, and that this capability would be incredibly useful. This combination of ambition and naivete is necessary for anyone to found a new company—how hard could it be?

Good advice for starting a company is to understand a customer problem, and then find a way to solve it using your unique capabilities. My cofounders, Damion Shelton and Mikhail Jones, and I did not do this. We relied on our belief that this technology would enable new possibilities and trusted ourselves to figure out the business as we went. So we simply focused on building our first product: the bipedal robot Cassie.

Cassie was the first dynamic bipedal robot that researchers could buy, able to maintain its balance through active, fluid motion rather than careful, rigid steps. It had ostrichlike legs, not because we were imitating ground-running birds, but as a result of engineering strictly for performance. It was not intended to be commercially useful, and had no torso, arms, or head. We sold Cassie robots to Harvard, Caltech, the University of Michigan, the University of California, Berkeley, and a handful of other research institutions, ultimately saturating the market for US $250,000 bipedal research robots after having sold a total of 10 of them.

ATRIAS, Cassie, and Digit 4 EVT [left to right] are on display at Agility Robotics’ RoboFab in Salem, Ore. The 70,000-square-foot facility has the capacity to produce more than 10,000 Digit 5 robots per year.Agility Robotics

Because Cassie’s hardware enabled research into the physics of walking and running, the legged-robot research frontier shifted to control software. Traditionally, engineers controlled legged robots with detailed mathematical models that determined how the machines should move. With Cassie, researchers pioneered the new approach of reinforcement learning for bipedal legged locomotion: A simulated robot learns through trial and error, and the resulting neural network controls the physical machine. This approach is what enables virtually all of the dynamic behaviors that you see on legged robots today, and Cassie looked alive as it recovered from stumbles while climbing stairs, ran 5 kilometers across the Oregon State campus, and broke the robot world record for a 100-meter dash.

Cassie got us closer to being able to move through the world with confidence and grace, but to make it useful, we needed manipulation. After exhaustively exploring different configurations, we found that an upright torso helped the robot balance, while two arms mounted near the top of the torso allowed it to pick up large objects and to catch itself when it fell. Digit 1, which added a torso and arms to the Cassie legs, was our first mobile manipulation robot, and another step on the path toward a product that could do useful work for commercial customers.

Why Digit Began With Warehouse Bins

As we explored the first applications for Digit, potential customers kept asking us: Why legs? And why a humanoid? These were tough questions for me to answer, because they exposed a core business reality: It didn’t matter to Agility Robotics if we solved a cool science problem in a beautiful way. What mattered to the business was solving real problems for customers.

After years of engagement with industry partners, we found one answer in warehouses and manufacturing facilities: moving bins. Bin handling is a clearly defined task where two arms are needed to lift large bins up high and legs are the best way to balance and move in narrow spaces. Because the task can vary widely from one deployment to another, it hasn’t been broadly addressed by single-purpose automation. Yet it was constrained enough to give Digit an economically viable first job while it developed a broader set of skills.

In 2019, Digit began demonstrating its capabilities to do real work. With Ford Motor Company, we showed how Digit 1 could carry packages from an autonomous vehicle to a front porch. We developed Digit 2 and 3 while working with a certain global package delivery company on moving and sorting cardboard boxes. Amazon tested Digit 4 on moving and stacking bins, and it became the world’s first commercially deployed humanoid at the logistics provider GXO. In 2024, Digit appeared on the cover of Time magazine.

Despite Digit’s apparent success, we began to run into conflicts between my dream and the needs of actual customers. We were no longer working with relatively patient university research labs. Agility has to sell robots to survive, and customers will only purchase robots that provide value. If bins weren’t moving, our customers were losing money. We spent a huge amount of time and effort keeping our first deployments operational, which arguably eliminated any profit we made. Yet this also kept our company learning and alive the way no lab demo ever could.

I had no idea how hard it would be, or that running a company would involve so many things that have nothing to do with solving technical problems: deployments across the country; shipping, service, and customer support; fundraising and investor relations; more fundraising; human resources and IT; developing fleet-management software; managing a supply chain; and even more fundraising. I had no experience with any of these things. My career had focused on solving the technical challenges of robots interacting with the world, and it turned out that was only a tiny piece of building a successful robotics company. But Agility was the only path I saw to continuing the technical work and having an impact.

Turning Digit Into a Product

I knew that Agility needed to focus more on robots as a product, but I didn’t know how to make that happen. Hiring the people we needed to run the company meant giving up an immense amount of control, but we had no other choice. We recruited a new executive team with the experience required to commercialize this new technology, and they quickly made changes that were both painful and necessary.

Digit versions 1, 2, and 3 [left to right] show the evolution of the robot from a dynamic walking platform into a useful mobile manipulator. Agility

We had intended the next revision of Digit, Digit 4 EVT (Engineering Validation and Test), to be a relatively minor upgrade. But Agility’s new leadership insisted that the robot was missing key features that were essential if Digit was going to become a real product. So Digit 4 EVT instead incorporated a series of major changes in a highly compressed timeline, such as larger batteries and system-wide upgrades for safety and regulatory compliance, which added enough mass to dramatically alter the robot’s appearance and capabilities.

While early Digits were headless, Agility Robotics was able to justify a head for Digit 4 to optimize antenna and camera placement, and it turned out to be surprisingly useful for human-robot interaction.Christie Hemm Klok

I could only watch as others brought their own talents to bear to make Digit into a successful product, in gut-wrenching ways that didn’t always align with my vision. There were some especially difficult times when I felt like there were compromises made that didn’t seem necessary, but making those decisions was no longer my sole responsibility. I had to accept that Digit had grown far beyond me, and look for ways of influencing decisions rather than directing them. In the moment, it was incredibly frustrating, as Digit 4 EVT took a few steps backward from my vision of how humanoids should look and move.

Agility is in our name because agility is core to the future of the company. I want Digit to be lithe and graceful. When people see Digit, I want them to like the robot, to understand what it can do at a glance, and to feel that it’s there to help. But with Digit 4 EVT, all of that was sacrificed to functionality, because of course it had to be—the customer just needs the robot to do the work. The design process became a ruthless triage, with aesthetics and elegance of movement being delayed over and over again in favor of brutal functionality. For an engineer whose mind lives more in the future than in the present, it has been hard for me to accept this trajectory. And yet, through Digit 4 EVT’s commercial deployments, we began to really understand specific applications and what they required. We mapped the first 10 use cases Digit would perform, and then began designing Digit 5 from scratch based on everything we had learned.

Digit 5

Digit 5 will be Agility’s first real step toward a general-purpose robot. It marks our transition from imagining what a future humanoid robot should be to designing a product around the realities of customer deployments. These realities include things like European CE regulatory compliance, North American UL electrical-safety certifications, and Federal Communications Commission limits for electromagnetic radiation—all of which felt tangential to my dream for Digit, but were absolute requirements.

Digit 5 is designed to be the first humanoid robot that can operate safely next to human coworkers while working 20 hours a day and lifting more than a human can.Christie Hemm Klok

Customer requirements helped us realize that safety in particular was one of the most critical barriers to scaling. In Digit 4’s commercial deployments, the robots had to work behind physical barriers, separated from humans at all times, to meet insurance and regulatory demands. This seemed silly to me, because I’ve never felt that our robots were dangerous, but we have to prove that they’re safe. And since keeping the robots in safety cages severely limited their usefulness, enabling Digit 5 to operate safely around people became a primary design goal. We spent two years on this challenge.

Digit 5 is designed to be the first humanoid robot that can operate safely next to human coworkers. It will rely on an array of sensors to locate nearby people in a manner that’s certifiably safe, and then take actions based on that information. As a person approaches, Digit 5 is programmed to stop what it’s doing, set down its payload, sit on the floor, and cut power to its motors before the person gets close enough to touch the robot. This conservative approach reduces the risk to nearby people in a verifiable way, and we believe it’s the only approach that makes sense as a first step toward working alongside humans.

Yet this strategy also feels like a massive slowdown on the path toward robots becoming part of everyday life. Enabling coexistence with humans has influenced almost every aspect of Digit 5’s design: the shape of the legs and the body, the safety-rated sensors within protective housings, the isolated computers dedicated to safety, and more. All of these features increase the robot’s complexity, power consumption, mass, and physical size.

Digit 5 is Agility’s largest, heaviest, strongest, and most capable humanoid robot worker.

The robot’s design was driven by safety, with integrated protection for the robot and for the humans it will work around.Agility Robotics

Weighing over 120 kg, Digit 5 is a huge robot. It needed to achieve the lifting limits recommended under the U.S. National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health guidelines for human workers, which include repeatedly lifting 23-kg bins and reaching shelves 1.75 meters high. Digit is designed to perform tasks like these for 20 hours a day—something no human can do. This requires motors with enough power and torque to lift the load, but also enough precision to delicately control the force Digit applies when it makes contact with the world. To power those motors, we needed a large battery and a dock for rapid autonomous charging. The dock will deliver 240 amperes at 48 volts, which is enough current to make its thick charging cables visibly wiggle under the induced magnetic forces, while powerful fans blow air through cooling channels in the robot’s torso to keep the battery from overheating. The battery and cooling system takes up about 75 percent of Digit’s torso, but it will allow the robot to operate for 90 minutes and fully recharge during a 9-minute break, enabling near-continuous work.

All of this extra bulk means that Digit 5 can no longer run or jump the way previous generations could, and the svelte form I imagined has become physically impossible. In some ways, Digit 5 feels more like a forklift than the graceful humanoid I set out to build. But looking at the situation rationally, I believe this trade-off is necessary for any company that claims its humanoid can do this kind of work today: If you see a robot that looks like a human working in a factory or warehouse, it either can’t lift the required weight or can’t make it through the whole shift. And if it’s not covered with sensors, it’s likely not safe to stand next to.

The most visible change with Digit 5 is that humanlike legs replace the ostrichlike legs of our earlier versions. While the “backward” leg configuration was optimized for walking and running, we discovered that it created problems with squatting because the ankle will strike the ground. Digit 5 will spend a lot of time lifting heavy objects from near the floor, so we used a humanoid leg configuration with knee and hip motors that both contribute torque to help the robot stand up again.

When Digit detects an approaching human, the robot will lower itself to the floor and cut power to its motors. Agility believes this is the only near-term approach to verifiably reduce risk when the robot is working near people.Agility Robotics

Other companies building humanoid robots have copied the human form without ever understanding its purpose. It’s very frustrating that, to an outside observer, it now looks like we discarded Agility’s distinctive leg design and simply did what everyone else was doing. Yet I know that we arrived at this shape based purely on functional engineering choices. Making a robot look like a human is the easy part—without the function to match, and the understanding of the physics underlying that function, the whole point of the human form may be lost.

With the power, battery life, and safety features that we are designing into Digit 5, we will have a truly useful robot. But it also compromises on some things that are core to my vision and mission. I understand why we made the choices we did and can justify them all, but together they leave me unsatisfied. It’s the curse of the engineer.

What Comes After Digit 5

I believe Digit 5 will be the scaling moment for Agility Robotics, the inflection point where we can begin deploying robots in large numbers. While the robot will continue carrying bins, our road map includes many more tasks, from picking individual items and tending machines, to preparing parts for assembly and shipping, and eventually doing assembly work itself. Its interchangeable tool interfaces and modular design will enable us to gradually upgrade its subsystems. It will be a platform for improvement, a source of data for future behavior training, and a viable product all at the same time.

Hurst stands between the previous version of Digit, Digit 4 [left], and Digit 5.Christie Hemm Klok

But I cannot love Digit 5. It’s the largest, heaviest, most expensive robot Agility will ever build, full of design compromises that enable it to be exactly the robot it needs to be right now rather than the robot I dreamed of. In the beginning, I envisioned steady progress on agility and dexterity, with each version becoming more dynamically capable. Instead, developing Digit 5 has required large detours to incorporate requirements that seemed unrelated to my original vision. However, I now recognize that tackling these challenges was always necessary. Customers and product requirements didn’t ruin my vision; they revealed what my vision was missing. This is how robots will achieve commercial success and make a real-world impact, which will bring me closer to my scientific dream as well.

We won’t have a humanoid that matches the capabilities of humans until it achieves that mastery of motion that inspired me to found Agility over a decade ago. I saw glimmers of it with the spring-mass locomotion of ATRIAS, and more glimmers with Cassie’s running gait.

I know that such mastery is physically possible with the tools and hardware that we have right now, and despite all of its compromises, Digit 5 will give us a practical foundation for pursuing that dream. I want every future version of Digit to be lighter and more graceful, to interact more naturally with humans, and to be better at manipulating objects and moving through the world, enabling robots to enter aspects of our lives that they haven’t been able to help with before. By the time I’m old enough to need assistance at home, I expect Digit will be up to the task.

With Digit 5, Agility has built a robot that will be useful in our world. Now I’m getting back to work to make it beautiful, too.

When one robot loves another robot very much, and they’re connected by a wire, they can get together and make a brand new robot! SFW.

[ JSK Lab ]

What happens when Microducks meet? They start to sing together. Each Microduck syncs with its neighbors over Bluetooth, then they compose a song on the fly, in harmony and in perfect time. There’s no score and no conductor. Two, three, or four ducks are enough for a choir to break out.

If Pollen isn’t selling Microducks in four packs for this exact reason, WHAT ARE THEY EVEN DOING!?

[ Pollen ]

In an internal test, Google DeepMind robotics researchers instructed Gemini 4 Argon to watch a video of a human playing cornhole. Using its video understanding and advanced reasoning capabilities, Gemini 4 built a virtual simulation in MuJoCo and accurately calculated the physics and whole-body control required for Apptronik’s Apollo 2 humanoid to sink seven consecutive shots in the real world. This Video-to-Sim-to-Real pipeline compresses weeks of manual modeling into a few hours, transforming ordinary videos into an infinite training ground for physical AI.

[ Google DeepMind ]

As of 11 October 2026, NASA’s Perseverance rover has driven 28.10 miles (45.22 kilometers), becoming the new off-world record-holder for total distance driven by any vehicle on the surface of another world. title: Q&A: Mars Perseverance Rover Sets a Distance Record
summary:
On 11 October, the Perseverance rover completed a drive that brought its total distance traveled on Mars to 28.10 miles (45.22 kilometers). This is a new record for Mars rovers, enabled in large part by Perseverance’s ability to drive with much more autonomy than its predecessors. Over the past five years, Perseverance’s autonomy software has been steadily upgraded, and to learn more about how the record was broken and what the future holds for the rover, we spoke with Mark Maimone, the Perseverance Robotic Operations Deputy Team Chief at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory, who designed and developed the self-driving software for Mars rovers Spirit, Opportunity, Curiosity, and Perseverance.

Before we talk about Perseverance, let’s pour one out for the previous record holder, Opportunity, which landed on Mars in January 2004 for a three-month mission and ended its epic journey 15 years later in February 2019. This NASA video compresses Opportunity’s entire mission into four minutes and gives a poignant sense of the incredible distance that this little rover traveled over its 15-year life on Mars, doing science as it went:

NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory/YouTube

Opportunity drove 45.16 kilometers until a planetary-scale dust storm stopped it in its tracks, appropriately enough, in Perseverance Valley.

On 18 February 2021, Perseverance joined NASA’s Curiosity rover on the red planet, carrying the Ingenuity helicopter tucked under its belly. Curiosity and Perseverance both ditched Opportunity’s solar panels for a radioisotope thermoelectric generator. Curiosity has been active on Mars since 2012.

Despite Curiosity’s nearly 10-year head start, Perseverance is the rover to first break Opportunity’s record. There are several reasons for Perseverance overtaking Opportunity—ruggedized wheels for one—but the biggest contributor is that Perseverance was built for autonomy.

Maimone shares how JPL added enough autonomy for its Mars rover to drive itself from 225 million km away without crashing.

This animation shows Perseverance’s point of view during a drive of 807 feet (246 meters) along the rim of Jezero Crater on 10 December 2025, the 1,709th Martian day, or sol, of the mission. Captured over 2 hours and 35 minutes, 53 Navigation Camera (Navcam) image pairs were combined with rover data on orientation, wheel speed, and steering angle, as well as data from Perseverance’s Inertial Measurement Unit, and placed into a 3D virtual environment. The result is this reconstruction with virtual frames inserted about every 4 inches (0.1 meters) of drive progress. JPL-Caltech/NASA

Let’s talk about rover autonomy on Mars. Even before Perseverance, rovers were driving themselves, right?

Mark Maimone: Yes! Sojourner [in 1997] had an early kind of autonomous behavior—for sensing, it used four laser stripes projected onto the surface, which it used to measure the height of 20 points in the terrain in front of it. It could steer around big obstacles, or even thread the needle between two things. It was a real autonomy system, which is very impressive considering its CPU was less than one megahertz.

With Spirit and Opportunity, I developed the autonomy for those rovers. Every time they drove, they would use 256 x 256 pixel stereo pairs to map the geometry of the terrain and find a safe route forward. Spirit actually ended up driving itself 23 percent of the time, which I was frankly shocked by, since it drove much more slowly in that mode. But using autonomy helped Spirit travel 50 percent faster than it otherwise could have. Opportunity and Curiosity both only used autonomous driving about 5 percent of the time. Perseverance is the first Mars rover that drives itself 90 percent of the time, with its enhanced autonomy system that includes a second processor with an FPGA to speed up extra image processing operations.

What was it like to let Perseverance drive itself for the first time?

Maimone: Perseverance is the culmination of decades of work on Mars rover autonomy, so seeing Perseverance use its AutoNav system to drive itself basically at full speed, up to 120 meters an hour, was incredible.

These two images taken by Perseverance’s hazard avoidance and navigation cameras show (at left) the very first AutoNav drive on Mars where the rover autonomously stopped before running into a rock pile, and (at right) the second AutoNav drive where the rover successfully steered around a rock.JPL-Caltech/NASA

Where are the humans in this process?

Maimone: The plan of where to go is specified by the science team, and then on the engineering side, the strategic route planning team develops a path to get us to that goal by guessing, based on lower-resolution maps from orbit, what the terrain is going to look like for the rover. Each day, a tactical operations team combines the strategic overall route with that day’s science goals to pick the actual route the rover will follow.

We want humans to keep doing long-range planning because that avoids wasting time. For example, we’ve learned that if we see sandy areas with intersecting waves or crests—not just ripples blown in one direction, but cross-ripples going in multiple directions—the rover tends to sink into terrain like that, so we tell the rover to keep out of those areas. The onboard autonomy only measures terrain shape, not terrain type, so it benefits from those location-based annotations.

We now have years of experience correlating images taken from orbit with images taken by the rover, and understanding how different kinds of terrain affect the drive. With the current orbiters at Mars, we sometimes get 25 centimeters resolution on orbital images. That’s still not quite enough to see all obstacles; there could be a big rock that doesn’t really show up on a scale of more than one or two pixels, making it very hard to notice. That is why you want to have autonomy on the rover, but the greater help we can give it at a high level, the faster we can reach our goals and the fewer potential delays we’ll encounter.

This orbital view shows a region of complex Martian terrain that Perseverance could not navigate autonomously. The blue line shows the path that human planners estimated, while the white line shows the path taken by the rover. The inset image, from Perseverance’s hazard avoidance camera, shows the rocky, sandy, and sloped terrain.Source images: Olivier Toupet, Masahiro Ono, et al.; JPL-Caltech/University of Arizona/NASA

What happens when the autonomy system on Perseverance fails?

Maimone: We ended up not using the autonomy at all for about two months in more complex terrain while we tuned things and wrote new software to deal with that new terrain we hadn’t encountered before. Some of those changes were relatively quick, and some required months of study. For example, one parameter is the maximum amount of slope that the robot is allowed to climb, because on steep slopes, there is a risk of the rover slipping sideways.

We landed inside Jezero Crater, which was very flat, and so for the first three years, most of our driving was at less than 14 degrees of slope. When we finally decided to leave the crater, we began to encounter other terrain at higher tilts with greater rock density, and the experience we gained allowed us to re-tune the parameters to allow the rover to traverse those more difficult terrains, with slopes of up to 24 degrees.

Rover autonomy in the age of AI

Late last year, you let Anthropic’s Claude AI plan a 400-meter drive for Perseverance. How did that go?

Maimone: We had the AI look at the orbital images and pick out a path for us, which became the starting point of the day’s rover planning operations. Typically, that starting path comes from the human rover planner team, but in this case, it was generated by AI. Humans were still in the loop; the team reviewed it and made a couple of adjustments. AI gave us a solid starting point that allowed us to make rapid progress, because it’s much easier to validate a path than to pick one from scratch.

NASA’s Perseverance Mars rover took this selfie on July 23, 2024. The selfie is composed of 62 images taken by the WATSON (Wide Angle Topographic Sensor for Operations and eNgineering) camera on the end of the rover’s robotic arm.JPL-Caltech/MSSS/NASA

Do you think humans will remain a necessary part of rover operations, or do you see the next generation of Mars rovers operating for weeks at a time without human assistance?

Maimone: One of the things that has held us back from driving very long distances autonomously is that as we drive, the rover accumulates uncertainty in its position. When the uncertainty grows, it means we have to stay farther away from areas that human rover planners have identified as being potentially dangerous, called “keep-out zones.” In some cases, the uncertainty gets high enough that the rover can’t plan a safe path, because the keep-out zones (which grow with the rover’s uncertainty) get too big.

We now have a new capability that we’ve added to Perseverance called Mars Global Localization. With this new technology that can shrink our uncertainty, we theoretically have the ability to go as long as we have resources to keep driving safely based on our maps and keep-out zones.

But to truly run a mission for weeks, you need to not only drive long distances, but also execute science operations autonomously. We have people here also looking at automating science operations by doing image processing onboard the rover to get a better understanding of what’s out there and where to focus the instruments’ attention. So I do think we are getting to the point where we can support long-period autonomous operations. It has been a slow evolution, but we have great capabilities now and a good understanding of what’s needed to make it work well.

As someone who has been involved with all of these Mars rovers—including one that got stuck—do you fundamentally trust Perseverance to operate autonomously?

Maimone: I do. We built the software, tested it, ran millions of simulations, and did lots of work in the field in many different test environments. It hasn’t steered us wrong yet. We’re looking forward to setting even bigger records.
